Eliakim
ē-lī'ă-kĭm
n. (Hezekiah's steward, the man given the key of the house of David; also the birth-name of king Jehoiakim)
From Hebrew 'Elyaqim, “God raises up”, from 'El, God, and qum, to rise or establish. The name is fulfilled precisely in Isa 22, where God says He will call His servant Eliakim and clothe him.

Biblical Definition

Two men named Eliakim matter, and they stand at opposite ends of the same century. The first is Hezekiah's steward, “which was over the household” (2Ki 18:18), who stood on the wall to answer Rabshakeh and afterward went in sackcloth to Isaiah. Isa 22 makes him a type. Shebna the self-important treasurer, hewing himself a sepulchre on high, is to be pulled down, and God says: “I will call my servant Eliakim the son of Hilkiah” (Isa 22:20), robe him, gird him, commit the government into his hand, and — the great verse — “the key of the house of David will I lay upon his shoulder; so he shall open, and none shall shut; and he shall shut, and none shall open” (Isa 22:22). The risen Christ takes those exact words to Himself in the letter to Philadelphia (Rev 3:7). Eliakim is a nail fastened in a sure place, a father to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, a steward of a house not his own. The second Eliakim is the son of Josiah, whom Pharaohnechoh made king “and turned his name to Jehoiakim” (2Ki 23:34) — a puppet renamed by the man who installed him, and the king who cut Jeremiah's scroll with a penknife and burned it. One Eliakim carried the key; the other burned the word.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) has no article for Eliakim; in sacred history it names the steward of Hezekiah's household and the son of Josiah whose name Pharaoh changed to Jehoiakim.

expand to see more

ELIAKIM, n. The son of Hilkiah, steward or governor of the household of Hezekiah king of Judah.

The name signifies God shall raise up, or whom God establishes.

He was sent with Shebna and Joah to treat with Rabshakeh, and afterward to Isaiah the prophet.

Isaiah foretold that the key of the house of David should be laid upon his shoulder.

Also, the son of Josiah, whom Pharaohnechoh made king and named Jehoiakim.

Key Scripture

2Ki 18:18 — "And when they had called to the king, there came out to them Eliakim the son of Hilkiah, which was over the household, and Shebna the scribe, and Joah the son of Asaph the recorder."

Isa 22:20 — "And it shall come to pass in that day, that I will call my servant Eliakim the son of Hilkiah:"

Isa 22:22 — "And the key of the house of David will I lay upon his shoulder; so he shall open, and none shall shut; and he shall shut, and none shall open."

2Ki 23:34 — "And Pharaohnechoh made Eliakim the son of Josiah king in the room of Josiah his father, and turned his name to Jehoiakim, and took Jehoahaz away: and he came to Egypt, and died there."

Modern Corruption

Isa 22:22 has been claimed by Rome as the charter of the papal keys; the risen Christ applies the verse to Himself, and He does not delegate the key He holds.

expand to see more

Roman apologetics reads Isa 22:22 as the Old Testament pattern behind Mat 16:19, and infers a perpetual office of prime minister of the kingdom, held by Peter and transmitted to his successors at Rome. The New Testament settles the identification itself, and not in Rome's favour: “These things saith he that is holy, he that is true, he that hath the key of David, he that openeth, and no man shutteth; and shutteth, and no man openeth” (Rev 3:7). The verse is applied to the Lord Jesus, in His own words, without qualification. What He gives the church in Mat 16 and 18 is the ministerial use of the keys — preaching and discipline, binding and loosing by declaring His word — which the Reformers understood and which belongs to the eldership of a local congregation, not to a single bishop over the whole. The 1689 Confession holds two offices in the church, elder and deacon, and no third above them.

The second thing is Shebna, who is the whole reason Eliakim is promoted. Shebna was over the house and was spending his office on his own monument. God's judgment on him is one of the most physical in the prophets: He will surely violently turn and toss him like a ball into a large country, “and there the chariots of thy glory shall be the shame of thy lord's house” (Isa 22:18). A steward exists for his master's house. When a man in office begins building his own name inside it, God has been known to replace him publicly, and to name his successor in advance.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew 'Elyaqim (H471), from 'El (H410), God, and qum (H6965), to arise; maphteach (H4668), a key.

expand to see more

Hebrew 'Elyaqim (H471) — Eliakim, “God raises up”; fulfilled literally in Isa 22:20.

Hebrew qum (H6965) — to rise, stand, establish; the root of the promise in the name.

Hebrew maphteach (H4668) — a key, an opener; laid upon the shoulder as a badge of office.

Hebrew 'al hab-bayith — “over the household”; the office of chief steward of the palace.

Greek kleis (G2807) — a key; used by the risen Christ of the key of David (Rev 3:7).

Usage

"“I will call my servant Eliakim” — a name that was also a prophecy."

"“The key of the house of David will I lay upon his shoulder” — the office Christ claims."

"“Turned his name to Jehoiakim” — a king renamed by the power that owned him."
